# kigumi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kigumi/0.1.0/kigumi/

## Expand description

Facade for the Kigumi framework. Application modules depend only on this crate.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use kigumi_core::`- [inventory](https://docs.rs/inventory/0.3.24/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/inventory/index.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Everything needed to define a module: `use kigumi::prelude::*;`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_acls.html)- acls
- Registers a module’s ACLs so a server collects them via `registered_acls()`. Use at module top level:`kigumi::register_acls!(ACLS);`where`ACLS: &'static [Acl]`.
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_action.html)- action
- Registers a state-transition action on a model, runnable via `POST /api/<model>/<id>/action/<name>`.`kigumi::register_action!("sale.order", "confirm", confirm_order, &["sales.user"]);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_compute.html)- compute
- Registers a compute function by name, so the engine runs it on write for fields declaring it.
Use at module top level: `kigumi::register_compute!("compute_total", compute_total);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_constraint.html)- constraint
- Registers a cross-record constraint (Odoo `@api.constrains`):`func`runs in the write transaction after the record + its children are written, and returns`Err(msg)`to reject (roll back) the write.`fields`are the triggers (empty = every write); list the WRITTEN fields and One2many field names that drive the invariant, plus any stored computed field it reads (those also trigger on update). Use at module top level:`kigumi::register_constraint!("account.move", &["line_ids"], check_balanced);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_external.html)- external
- Marks a model’s table as owned outside the metamodel (Odoo’s `_auto = False`): the model is resolved/served normally but migration never creates or alters its table. For models mapped onto a pre-existing table (e.g.`res.users`onto the auth subsystem’s`kigumi_user`) or a SQL view. Use at module top level:`kigumi::register_external!("res.users");`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_field_groups.html)- field_ - groups
- Restricts a model field to the given groups (D6 field-level security): read AND write of that
field require membership in at least one group; superuser bypasses. Usually emitted automatically
by `#[field(groups = "...")]`, but can be declared by hand:`kigumi::register_field_groups!("res.users", "login", &["admin"]);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_inherits.html)- inherits
- Declares delegation inheritance (Odoo’s `_inherits`):`model`exposes`parent`’s stored scalar fields through its required Many2one`via`FK. Usually emitted by`#[model(inherits=…, via=…)]`:`kigumi::register_inherits!("product.product", "product.template", "product_tmpl_id");`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_job.html)- job
- Registers a BACKGROUND JOB kind, runnable ad hoc with retries: enqueue with
`Db::enqueue_job(name, payload)`or — transactionally, inside a service — with`ServiceCtx::enqueue_job`.`func`is an`async fn(&Db, Json) -> Result<(), DbError>`; a returned Err retries with exponential backoff up to`max_attempts`(then dead-letters). Bodies MUST be idempotent (at-least-once execution).`kigumi::register_job!("send_invoice_mail", 8, send_mail);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_ledger_report.html)- ledger_ - report
- Registers a read-only LEDGER REPORT (record-less aggregate query, returning JSON rows) runnable via
`GET /api/reports/<name>`— distinct from`register_report!`, which is the per-record document/PDF engine.`func`is an`async fn(&PgPool, params) -> Result<Vec<Json>, DbError>`;`read_model`is the model whose Read ACL gates it. The macro emits the one`Box::pin`adapting the async fn to the fn ptr.`kigumi::register_ledger_report!("trial_balance", "account.account", trial_balance, &[]);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_mailed.html)- mailed
- Opts a model into the mail subsystem (chatter): it gains a thread of messages, followers and
activities via the `(res_model, res_id)`link, and the framework cleans that thread up when the record is deleted. One line, no mixin:`kigumi::register_mailed!("sale.order");`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_migration.html)- migration
- Registers a versioned DATA migration for a module — the upgrade contract. It runs when migrate
finds the module installed at a ledger version < `to_version`while the linked crate is
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_module.html)- module
- Registers a module’s manifest in the global catalog, so `resolve_modules`can see it. Use at module top level:`kigumi::register_module!(MANIFEST);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_related.html)- related
- Marks a field as a `related`field (Odoo`related=`): a non-stored, read-only mirror of the value reached by`path`(e.g. “order_id.currency_id”). Usually emitted by`#[field(related = "...")]`.`kigumi::register_related!("sale.order.line", "order_currency_id", "order_id.currency_id");`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_report.html)- report
- Registers a report on a model: a pure render fn producing an HTML document for one record, exposed
at `GET /api/<model>/<id>/report/<name>`(secured by read access to the record) and listed in the model’s UI contract.`name`is the URL segment,`title`the human label. Use at module top level:`kigumi::register_report!("sale.order", "quotation", "Quotation", render_quotation);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_route.html)- route
- Registers a MODULE HTTP ROUTE on the generic dispatch `GET|POST /api/x/<name>`— bespoke module endpoints (an inbound-webhook receiver, a custom search) without the module ever depending on the server crate or axum.`method`is a RouteMethod variant name (Get|Post);`auth: false`runs the body under the GUEST context (uid −1, no groups — the default-deny ACL blocks every secured call, so verify the sender yourself — use`RouteInput::verify_hmac_sha256`or your provider’s exact scheme with a CONSTANT-TIME comparison, never a hand-rolled hash +`==`— then elevate via`.sudo()`. Query/body/header values are anonymous input: bind them in SQL, never interpolate).`kigumi::register_route!("stripe-hook", Post, false, &[], stripe_hook);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_rules.html)- rules
- Registers a module’s record rules so a server collects them via `registered_rules()`. Use at module top level:`kigumi::register_rules!(RULES);`where`RULES: &'static [RecordRule]`.
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_seed.html)- seed
- Registers a module’s idempotent reference-data seeder, run at every migrate while the module
is installed (in dependency order). Bodies must never overwrite operator changes — guard with
count/exists checks: the DB is the authority. `func`is an`async fn(&Db) -> Result<(), DbError>`.`kigumi::register_seed!("base", seed::seed_base_data);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_sequence.html)- sequence
- Registers a document-numbering sequence, declared by the module whose action consumes it
(`ActionOutcome::assign_sequence`). Ensured at migrate; an existing sequence keeps its counter.`kigumi::register_sequence!("sales", "SO", "SO/", "", 5);`→ SO/00001.
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_service.html)- service
- Registers a cross-record SERVICE on a model, runnable via `POST /api/<model>/<id>/service/<name>`. The transactional twin of`register_action!`:`func`is a`async fn(&mut ServiceCtx, ServiceInput) -> Result<ServiceOutput, DbError>`that owns multi-record logic through the secured`ServiceCtx`.`write_gate`is`true`for a mutating service,`false`for a read-only one (a report). The macro emits the one`Box::pin`that adapts the async fn to the stored fn pointer.`kigumi::register_service!("sale.order.discount", "apply_discount", apply_discount, true, &["sales.user"]);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_tracked.html)- tracked
- Marks a field as tracked (Odoo’s `tracking=True`): a change to it on a mailed model records a`notification`message + a typed`mail.tracking`row in the chatter. Usually emitted by`#[field(tracked)]`, but can be declared by hand:`kigumi::register_tracked!("sale.order", "state");`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_transient.html)- transient
- Marks a model as transient (Odoo’s `TransientModel`): a wizard scratchpad whose rows are ephemeral. The model is served + secured like any model, but an hourly GC cron reclaims rows by age, and migration gives its`create_date`column a`DEFAULT now()`so every insert is stamped. The model must declare a nullable`create_date: Datetime`. One line:`kigumi::register_transient!("sale.order.discount");`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_view.html)- view
- Registers a model’s form layout (Odoo’s form arch, minimal): titled groups of scalar fields plus a
notebook of tabbed pages. Emitted in the model’s UI contract so the frontend renders a real view
instead of dumping fields in declaration order. Use at module top level:
`kigumi::register_view!("product.product", &[ FieldGroup { .. } ], &[ NotebookPage { .. } ]);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_wizard.html)- wizard
- Registers a wizard: binds a transient `model`to its`default_get`(the server-side seed computed from the open context), exposing`POST /api/<model>/open`. The model must also be`register_transient!`-marked. Apply logic is a dedicated per-wizard service method + endpoint (like`apply_pricelist`), not part of this registration. Use at module top level:`kigumi::register_wizard!("sale.order.discount", default_get_discount);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_write_trigger.html)- write_ - trigger
- Registers an in-tx WRITE TRIGGER: `func`runs on the caller’s transaction after a secured write to`model`when one of`watch`columns changed (empty = every write), for a stored effect the`depends`recompute can’t express on read — e.g. a Many2many aggregate summed across a join.`func`is an`async fn(&mut Transaction, id, changed_cols) -> Result<(), DbError>`; a returned`Err`rolls the write back. The macro emits the one`Box::pin`adapting the async fn to the stored fn pointer.`kigumi::register_write_trigger!("product.template.attribute.value", &["price_extra"], recompute);`

# dcb_layer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/dcb-layer/0.2.1/dcb_layer/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#dcb)dcb

A [DCB-compliant](https://dcb.events) event store backed by [FoundationDB](https://www.foundationdb.org).

Events are appended atomically, assigned a globally ordered [ Versionstamp](https://docs.rs/type.Versionstamp.html) position,
and indexed for fast retrieval by type, tags, or both.
Optimistic concurrency is enforced through

[s that fail the write if matching events appeared since the caller last read.](https://docs.rs/struct.AppendCondition.html)

`AppendCondition`[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

```
use dcb_layer::{Event, FdbStore, Query, QueryItem};
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // 1. Open a FoundationDB database (see foundationdb-rs for setup).
    let _network = unsafe { foundationdb::boot() };
    let db = foundationdb::Database::default().unwrap();
    // 2. Create a namespaced store — namespace isolates data within one FDB cluster.
    let store = FdbStore::new(db, "my-app");
    // 3. Append events (no condition = unconditional write).
    let event = Event::new(
        "OrderPlaced",
        ["order:42", "customer:7"],
        b"{\"total\":99}".as_slice(),
    );
    let position = store.append(vec![event], vec![]).await.unwrap();
    // 4. Read events back — filter by type, tags, or both.
    let results = store
        .read(
            Query {
                items: vec![QueryItem {
                    types: vec!["OrderPlaced".into()],
                    tags: vec!["customer:7".into()],
                }],
            },
            None,
        )
        .await
        .unwrap();
    println!("Found {} event(s), first at {:?}", results.len(), results[0].position);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#core-concepts)Core concepts

[§](https://docs.rs#event)Event

An [ Event](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html) carries three fields, constructed via

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html#method.new)

`Event::new`| Field | Accepts | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `type_name` | `&str`/`String` | Required, non-empty (e.g. `"OrderPlaced"`) |
| `tags` | any iterable of strings | Up to 10 tags; `"_"`is reserved |
| `data` | `&[u8]`/`Vec<u8>` | Opaque bytes — encode however you like |

Tags are free-form strings. A common convention is `"entity:id"` (e.g. `"order:42"`),
but the store treats them as opaque labels.

[§](https://docs.rs#query)Query

A [ Query](https://docs.rs/struct.Query.html) is a list of

[s joined by](https://docs.rs/struct.QueryItem.html)

`QueryItem`**OR**. Each item matches events that satisfy

**all**of its constraints:

- `types`— event’s- `type_name`must be one of these (empty = any type)
- `tags`— event must carry- **all**of these tags (empty = any tags)

Every item must specify at least one type or one tag.

```
use dcb_layer::{Query, QueryItem};
// Match OrderPlaced OR OrderCancelled events tagged with order:42
let query = Query {
    items: vec![
        QueryItem { types: vec!["OrderPlaced".into()], tags: vec!["order:42".into()] },
        QueryItem { types: vec!["OrderCancelled".into()], tags: vec!["order:42".into()] },
    ],
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#appendcondition)AppendCondition

An [ AppendCondition](https://docs.rs/struct.AppendCondition.html) guards a write with an optimistic-concurrency check:
the

`append` call fails with [if any event matching](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html#variant.AppendConditionFailed)

`Error::AppendConditionFailed``query` exists **after**the

`after` position (or at all, when `after` is `None`).The typical pattern:

- Read events matching your query → note the last position seen.
- Build your decision model from those events.
- Append new events with `after = last_position`to guard against concurrent writes.

```
use dcb_layer::{AppendCondition, Event, FdbStore, Query, QueryItem};
// 1. Read events and note the last position seen.
let results = store.read(
    Query { items: vec![QueryItem { types: vec!["OrderPlaced".into()], tags: vec!["order:42".into()] }] },
    None,
).await.unwrap();
let last_position = results.last().map(|e| e.position);
// 2. Append new events — fail if a concurrent write snuck in after last_position.
let condition = AppendCondition {
    query: Query {
        items: vec![QueryItem {
            types: vec!["OrderPlaced".into()],
            tags: vec!["order:42".into()],
        }],
    },
    after: last_position,
};
store.append(vec![Event::new("OrderPlaced", ["order:42"], b"".as_slice())], vec![condition]).await.unwrap();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#readoptions)ReadOptions

[ ReadOptions](https://docs.rs/struct.ReadOptions.html) controls pagination and ordering:

| Field | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `limit` | `0`(unlimited) | Maximum events to return |
| `after` | `None` | Only return events after this position |
| `reverse` | `false` | Newest-first when `true` |

[§](https://docs.rs#limits)Limits

| Constraint | Value |
|---|---|
| Max events per `append`call | 65 535 |
| Max tags per event | 10 |
| Reserved tag value | `"_"` |

[§](https://docs.rs#practical-sizing)Practical sizing

Each event writes one index key per **subset** of its tags (2^n keys for
n tags — up to 1 024 for 10 tags). All writes of an `append` call share one
FDB transaction, which is capped at 10 MB of affected data and 5 seconds —
keep batches small when events carry many tags.

Reads run in a single FDB transaction too: an unbounded [ FdbStore::read](https://docs.rs/struct.FdbStore.html#method.read)
or

[over a large store fails with](https://docs.rs/struct.FdbStore.html#method.read_all)

`FdbStore::read_all``transaction_too_old` (FDB error 1007) after a bounded number of retries.
Paginate with

`ReadOptions``limit` + `after`.Subscription cursors ([ FdbStore::set_cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.FdbStore.html#method.set_cursor)) are last-writer-wins; run
one consumer per cursor name or coordinate externally.

[§](https://docs.rs#foundationdb-setup)FoundationDB setup

This crate wraps the [ foundationdb](https://docs.rs/foundationdb) crate.
You are responsible for:

- installing and running an FDB cluster
- calling `unsafe { foundationdb::boot() }`once at startup (keeps the network thread alive)
- opening a `foundationdb::Database``FdbStore::new`

Refer to the [foundationdb-rs documentation](https://docs.rs/foundationdb) and
the [FoundationDB developer guide](https://apple.github.io/foundationdb/getting-started-linux.html)
for cluster setup and client configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#fdb-api-version)FDB API version

The default Cargo feature targets FDB 7.4. To use FDB 7.3, disable the default features:

`dcb-layer = { version = "...", default-features = false, features = ["fdb-7_3"] }`The feature selects the C API headers compiled against; a newer `libfdb_c` is backward compatible.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Versionstamp](https://docs.rs/type.Versionstamp.html)
- 12-byte globally unique, monotonically increasing position. Bytes 0–9: FDB transaction version (big-endian). Bytes 10–11: user version = batch index (big-endian u16).

# rend 0.5.4 - Docs.rs

rend provides cross-platform, endian-aware primitives for Rust.

## Documentation

## Example

```
use transmute;
use *;
let little_int = from_native;
// Internal representation is little-endian
assert_eq!;
// Can also be made with `.into()`
let little_int: i32_le = 0x12345678.into;
// Still formats correctly
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
let big_int = from_native;
// Internal representation is big-endian
assert_eq!;
// Can also be made with `.into()`
let big_int: i32_be = 0x12345678.into;
// Still formats correctly
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```

# rend 0.5.4 - Docs.rs

                    rend 0.5.4

                Cross-platform, endian-aware primitives for Rust

---

# rend - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rend/0.5.4/target-redirect/rend/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rend)rend

rend provides cross-platform, endian-aware primitives for Rust.

rend does not provide cross-platform alternatives for types that are
inherently cross-platform, such as `bool` and `u8`. It also does not provide
cross-platform alternatives for types that have an architecture-dependent
size, such as `isize` and `usize`. rend does not support custom types.

rend is intended to be used to build portable types that can be shared between different architectures.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `bytecheck`: Enables support for validating types using- `bytecheck`.

[§](https://docs.rs#crates)Crates

- `zerocopy-0_8`

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example:

```
use core::mem::transmute;
use rend::*;
let little_int = i32_le::from_native(0x12345678);
// Internal representation is little-endian
assert_eq!(
    [0x78, 0x56, 0x34, 0x12],
    unsafe { transmute::<_, [u8; 4]>(little_int) }
);
// Can also be made with `.into()`
let little_int: i32_le = 0x12345678.into();
// Still formats correctly
assert_eq!("305419896", format!("{}", little_int));
assert_eq!("0x12345678", format!("0x{:x}", little_int));
let big_int = i32_be::from_native(0x12345678);
// Internal representation is big-endian
assert_eq!(
    [0x12, 0x34, 0x56, 0x78],
    unsafe { transmute::<_, [u8; 4]>(big_int) }
);
// Can also be made with `.into()`
let big_int: i32_be = 0x12345678.into();
// Still formats correctly
assert_eq!("305419896", format!("{}", big_int));
assert_eq!("0x12345678", format!("0x{:x}", big_int));
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [unaligned](https://docs.rs/unaligned/index.html)
- Cross-platform primitives with unaligned representations.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Atomic](https://docs.rs/struct.AtomicI16_be.html)- I16_ - be
- A big-endian `AtomicI16`with a guaranteed size and alignment of`2`.
- [Atomic](https://docs.rs/struct.AtomicI16_le.html)- I16_ - le
- A little-endian `AtomicI16`with a guaranteed size and alignment of`2`.
- [Atomic](https://docs.rs/struct.AtomicI32_be.html)- I32_ - be

# rend - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rend/0.5.4/rend/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rend)rend

rend provides cross-platform, endian-aware primitives for Rust.

rend does not provide cross-platform alternatives for types that are
inherently cross-platform, such as `bool` and `u8`. It also does not provide
cross-platform alternatives for types that have an architecture-dependent
size, such as `isize` and `usize`. rend does not support custom types.

rend is intended to be used to build portable types that can be shared between different architectures.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `bytecheck`: Enables support for validating types using- `bytecheck`.

[§](https://docs.rs#crates)Crates

- `zerocopy-0_8`

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example:

```
use core::mem::transmute;
use rend::*;
let little_int = i32_le::from_native(0x12345678);
// Internal representation is little-endian
assert_eq!(
    [0x78, 0x56, 0x34, 0x12],
    unsafe { transmute::<_, [u8; 4]>(little_int) }
);
// Can also be made with `.into()`
let little_int: i32_le = 0x12345678.into();
// Still formats correctly
assert_eq!("305419896", format!("{}", little_int));
assert_eq!("0x12345678", format!("0x{:x}", little_int));
let big_int = i32_be::from_native(0x12345678);
// Internal representation is big-endian
assert_eq!(
    [0x12, 0x34, 0x56, 0x78],
    unsafe { transmute::<_, [u8; 4]>(big_int) }
);
// Can also be made with `.into()`
let big_int: i32_be = 0x12345678.into();
// Still formats correctly
assert_eq!("305419896", format!("{}", big_int));
assert_eq!("0x12345678", format!("0x{:x}", big_int));
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [unaligned](https://docs.rs/unaligned/index.html)
- Cross-platform primitives with unaligned representations.

[195](#195)macro_rules! define_char {
[196](#196)    ($name:ident: $endian:ident) => {
[197](#197)        define_newtype!(
[198](#198)            #[cfg_attr(
[199](#199)                feature = "zerocopy-0_8",
[200](#200)                derive(
[201](#201)                    zerocopy_derive::IntoBytes,
[210](#210)                    zerocopy_derive::Immutable,
[211](#211)                    zerocopy_derive::KnownLayout,
[212](#212)                ),
[213](#213)            )]
[214](#214)            $name: $endian 4 u32
[215](#215)        );
[216](#216)        impl_char!($name: $endian);
[217](#217)
[218](#218)        #[cfg(feature = "bytecheck")]
[219](#219)        unsafe impl<C> bytecheck::CheckBytes<C> for $name
[222](#222)        where
[223](#223)            C: bytecheck::rancor::Fallible + ?Sized,
[224](#224)            C::Error: bytecheck::rancor::Trace,
[225](#225)            char: bytecheck::CheckBytes<C>,
[226](#226)        {
[227](#227)            #[inline]
[228](#228)            unsafe fn check_bytes(
[229](#229)                value: *const Self,
[230](#230)                context: &mut C,
[231](#231)            ) -> Result<(), C::Error> {
[232](#232)                use bytecheck::rancor::ResultExt as _;
[233](#233)
[234](#234)                let u = unsafe { *value.cast::<u32>() };
[237](#237)                let c = swap_endian!($endian u);
[238](#238)                unsafe {
[241](#241)                    char::check_bytes(&c as *const u32 as *const char, context)
[242](#242)                        .with_trace(|| $crate::context::ValueCheckContext {
[243](#243)                            inner_name: "char",
[244](#244)                            outer_name: core::stringify!($name),
[245](#245)                        })
[246](#246)                }
[247](#247)            }
[248](#248)        }
[249](#249)    };
[250](#250)}

[278](#278)        where

[280](#280)            C::Error: bytecheck::rancor::Trace,
[281](#281)            $prim: bytecheck::CheckBytes<C>,

[285](#285)                value: *const Self,

[295](#295)                    <$prim>::check_bytes(value.cast(), context)
[296](#296)                        .with_trace(|| $crate::context::ValueCheckContext {

[329](#329)#[allow(dead_code)]
[330](#330)const fn fetch_ordering(order: Ordering) -> Ordering {
[331](#331)    match order {
[332](#332)        Ordering::Relaxed => Ordering::Relaxed,
[333](#333)        Ordering::Release => Ordering::Relaxed,
[334](#334)        Ordering::Acquire => Ordering::Acquire,
[335](#335)        Ordering::AcqRel => Ordering::Acquire,
[336](#336)        Ordering::SeqCst => Ordering::SeqCst,
[337](#337)        order => order,
[338](#338)    }
[339](#339)}
[340](#340)
[341](#341)#[cfg(any(
[342](#342)    target_has_atomic = "16",
[343](#343)    target_has_atomic = "32",
[344](#344)    target_has_atomic = "64",
[345](#345)))]
[346](#346)macro_rules! define_atomic {
[347](#347)    (
[348](#348)        $name:ident:
[349](#349)        $endian:ident $size_align:literal $prim:ty as $prim_int:ty
[350](#350)    ) => {
[351](#351)        define_newtype!(
[352](#352)            #[cfg_attr(
[353](#353)                feature = "zerocopy-0_8",
[354](#354)                derive(
[355](#355)                    zerocopy_derive::FromBytes,
[356](#356)                    zerocopy_derive::IntoBytes,
[357](#357)                    zerocopy_derive::KnownLayout,
[358](#358)                ),
[359](#359)            )]
[360](#360)            $name: $endian $size_align $prim
[361](#361)        );
[362](#362)
[363](#363)        impl $name {
[364](#364)            #[doc = concat!(
[365](#365)                "Returns a `",
[366](#366)                stringify!($name),
[367](#367)                "` containing `value`.",
[368](#368)            )]
[369](#369)            #[inline]
[370](#370)            pub const fn new(value: $prim_int) -> Self {
[371](#371)                Self(<$prim>::new(swap_endian!($endian value)))
[372](#372)            }
[373](#373)        }
[374](#374)
[375](#375)        unsafe_impl_check_bytes_noop!(for $name);
[378](#378)
[379](#379)        impl $name {
[380](#380)            #[doc = concat!(
[384](#384)                "See [`",
[385](#385)                stringify!($prim),
[386](#386)                "::compare_exchange`] for more information.",
[387](#387)            )]
[388](#388)            #[inline]
[389](#389)            pub fn compare_exchange(
[390](#390)                &self,
[391](#391)                current: $prim_int,
[392](#392)                new: $prim_int,
[393](#393)                success: Ordering,
[394](#394)                failure: Ordering,
[395](#395)            ) -> Result<$prim_int, $prim_int> {
[396](#396)                match self.0.compare_exchange(
[397](#397)                    swap_endian!($endian current),
[398](#398)                    swap_endian!($endian new),
[399](#399)                    success,
[400](#400)                    failure,
[401](#401)                ) {
[402](#402)                    Ok(x) => Ok(swap_endian!($endian x)),
[403](#403)                    Err(x) => Err(swap_endian!($endian x)),
[404](#404)                }
[405](#405)            }
[406](#406)
[407](#407)            #[doc = concat!(
[411](#411)                "See [`",
[412](#412)                stringify!($prim),
[413](#413)                "::compare_exchange_weak`] for more information.",
[414](#414)            )]
[415](#415)            #[inline]
[416](#416)            pub fn compare_exchange_weak(
[417](#417)                &self,
[418](#418)                current: $prim_int,
[419](#419)                new: $prim_int,
[420](#420)                success: Ordering,
[421](#421)                failure: Ordering,
[422](#422)            ) -> Result<$prim_int, $prim_int> {
[423](#423)                match self.0.compare_exchange_weak(
[424](#424)                    swap_endian!($endian current),
[425](#425)                    swap_endian!($endian new),
[426](#426)                    success,
[427](#427)                    failure,
[428](#428)                ) {
[429](#429)                    Ok(x) => Ok(swap_endian!($endian x)),
[430](#430)                    Err(x) => Err(swap_endian!($endian x)),
[431](#431)                }
[432](#432)            }
[433](#433)
[434](#434)            #[doc = concat!(
[437](#437)                "Because addition is not an endian-agnostic operation, ",
[438](#438)                "`fetch_add` is implemented in terms of [`",
[439](#439)                stringify!($prim),
[440](#440)                "::compare_exchange_weak`] on ",
[441](#441)                opposite_endian_name!($endian),
[442](#442)                "-endian targets. This may result in worse performance on ",
[443](#443)                "those targets.",
[444](#444)            )]
[445](#445)            #[doc = concat!(
[447](#447)                "See [`",
[448](#448)                stringify!($prim),
[449](#449)                "::fetch_add`] for more information.",
[450](#450)            )]
[451](#451)            #[inline]
[452](#452)            pub fn fetch_add(
[453](#453)                &self,
[454](#454)                val: $prim_int,
[455](#455)                order: Ordering,
[456](#456)            ) -> $prim_int {
[457](#457)                if_native_endian!(
[458](#458)                    $endian
[459](#459)                    self.0.fetch_add(val, order),
[460](#460)                    self.fetch_update_fast(
[461](#461)                        order,
[462](#462)                        fetch_ordering(order),
[463](#463)                        |x| x + val,
[464](#464)                    ),
[465](#465)                )
[466](#466)            }
[467](#467)

[482](#482)                swap_endian!($endian self.0.fetch_and(val, order))
[483](#483)            }

[602](#602)                "::fetch_sub`] for more information.",
[603](#603)            )]
[604](#604)            #[inline]
[605](#605)            pub fn fetch_sub(
[606](#606)                &self,
[607](#607)                val: $prim_int,
[608](#608)                order: Ordering,
[609](#609)            ) -> $prim_int {
[610](#610)                if_native_endian!(
[611](#611)                    $endian
[612](#612)                    self.0.fetch_sub(val, order),
[613](#613)                    self.fetch_update_fast(
[614](#614)                        order,
[615](#615)                        fetch_ordering(order),
[616](#616)                        |x| x - val,
[617](#617)                    ),
[618](#618)                )
[619](#619)            }
[620](#620)
[621](#621)            #[allow(dead_code)]
[622](#622)            #[inline(always)]
[623](#623)            fn fetch_update_fast<F: Fn($prim_int) -> $prim_int>(
[624](#624)                &self,
[625](#625)                set_order: Ordering,
[626](#626)                fetch_order: Ordering,
[627](#627)                f: F,
[628](#628)            ) -> $prim_int {
[629](#629)                let mut prev = self.load(fetch_order);
[630](#630)                loop {
[631](#631)                    let next = f(prev);
[632](#632)                    match self.compare_exchange_weak(
[633](#633)                        prev,
[634](#634)                        next,
[635](#635)                        set_order,
[636](#636)                        fetch_order,
[637](#637)                    ) {
[638](#638)                        Ok(x) => break x,
[639](#639)                        Err(next_prev) => {
[640](#640)                            prev = next_prev;
[641](#641)                        }
[642](#642)                    }
[643](#643)                }
[644](#644)            }
[645](#645)
[646](#646)            #[doc = concat!(
[651](#651)                "See [`",
[652](#652)                stringify!($prim),
[653](#653)                "::fetch_update`] for more information.",
[654](#654)            )]
[655](#655)            #[inline]
[656](#656)            pub fn fetch_update<F: FnMut($prim_int) -> Option<$prim_int>>(
[657](#657)                &self,
[658](#658)                set_order: Ordering,
[659](#659)                fetch_order: Ordering,
[660](#660)                mut f: F,
[661](#661)            ) -> Result<$prim_int, $prim_int> {
[662](#662)                self.0.fetch_update(set_order, fetch_order, |x| {
[663](#663)                    f(swap_endian!($endian x)).map(|y| swap_endian!($endian y))
[664](#664)                })
[665](#665)            }
[666](#666)
[667](#667)            #[doc = concat!(
[670](#670)                "See [`",
[671](#671)                stringify!($prim),
[672](#672)                "::fetch_xor`] for more information.",
[673](#673)            )]
[674](#674)            #[inline]
[675](#675)            pub fn fetch_xor(
[676](#676)                &self,
[677](#677)                val: $prim_int,
[678](#678)                order: Ordering,
[679](#679)            ) -> $prim_int {
[680](#680)                let val = swap_endian!($endian val);
[681](#681)                swap_endian!($endian self.0.fetch_xor(val, order))
[682](#682)            }
[683](#683)
[684](#684)            #[doc = concat!(
[687](#687)                "See [`",
[688](#688)                stringify!($prim),
[689](#689)                "::into_inner`] for more information.",
[690](#690)            )]
[691](#691)            #[inline]
[692](#692)            pub fn into_inner(self) -> $prim_int {
[693](#693)                swap_endian!($endian self.0.into_inner())
[694](#694)            }
[695](#695)
[696](#696)            #[doc = concat!(
[699](#699)                "See [`",
[700](#700)                stringify!($prim),
[701](#701)                "::load`] for more information.",
[702](#702)            )]
[703](#703)            #[inline]
[704](#704)            pub fn load(&self, order: Ordering) -> $prim_int {
[705](#705)                swap_endian!($endian self.0.load(order))
[706](#706)            }
[707](#707)
[708](#708)            #[doc = concat!(
[711](#711)                "See [`",
[712](#712)                stringify!($prim),
[713](#713)                "::store`] for more information.",
[714](#714)            )]
[715](#715)            #[inline]
[716](#716)            pub fn store(&self, val: $prim_int, order: Ordering) {
[717](#717)                self.0.store(swap_endian!($endian val), order);
[718](#718)            }
[719](#719)
[720](#720)            #[doc = concat!(
[724](#724)                "See [`",
[725](#725)                stringify!($prim),
[726](#726)                "::swap`] for more information.",
[727](#727)            )]
[728](#728)            #[inline]
[729](#729)            pub fn swap(&self, val: $prim_int, order: Ordering) -> $prim_int {
[730](#730)                let val = swap_endian!($endian val);
[731](#731)                swap_endian!($endian self.0.swap(val, order))
[732](#732)            }
[733](#733)        }
[734](#734)
[735](#735)        impl core::fmt::Debug for $name {
[736](#736)            #[inline]
[737](#737)            fn fmt(
[738](#738)                &self,
[739](#739)                f: &mut core::fmt::Formatter<'_>,
[740](#740)            ) -> core::fmt::Result {
[741](#741)                swap_endian!($endian self.load(Ordering::Relaxed)).fmt(f)
[742](#742)            }
[743](#743)        }
[744](#744)
[745](#745)        impl Default for $name {
[746](#746)            #[inline]
[747](#747)            fn default() -> Self {
[748](#748)                Self::new(<$prim_int>::default())
[749](#749)            }
[750](#750)        }
[751](#751)
[752](#752)        impl From<$prim_int> for $name {
[753](#753)            #[inline]
[754](#754)            fn from(value: $prim_int) -> Self {
[755](#755)                Self::new(value)
[756](#756)            }
[757](#757)        }
[758](#758)    }
[759](#759)}
[760](#760)
[761](#761)#[cfg(any(
[762](#762)    target_has_atomic = "16",
[763](#763)    target_has_atomic = "32",
[764](#764)    target_has_atomic = "64",
[765](#765)))]
[766](#766)macro_rules! define_atomics {
[767](#767)    ($(
[768](#768)        $le:ident $be:ident:
[769](#769)        $size_align:literal $prim:ty as $prim_int:ty
[770](#770)    ),* $(,)?) => {
[771](#771)        $(
[772](#772)            define_atomic!($le: little $size_align $prim as $prim_int);
[773](#773)            define_atomic!($be: big $size_align $prim as $prim_int);
[774](#774)        )*
[775](#775)    }
[776](#776)}
[777](#777)
[778](#778)#[cfg(target_has_atomic = "16")]
[779](#779)define_atomics! {
[780](#780)    AtomicI16_le AtomicI16_be: 2 AtomicI16 as i16,
[781](#781)    AtomicU16_le AtomicU16_be: 2 AtomicU16 as u16,
[782](#782)}
[783](#783)
[784](#784)#[cfg(target_has_atomic = "32")]
[785](#785)define_atomics! {
[786](#786)    AtomicI32_le AtomicI32_be: 4 AtomicI32 as i32,
[787](#787)    AtomicU32_le AtomicU32_be: 4 AtomicU32 as u32,
[788](#788)}
[789](#789)
[790](#790)#[cfg(target_has_atomic = "64")]
[791](#791)define_atomics! {
[792](#792)    AtomicI64_le AtomicI64_be: 8 AtomicI64 as i64,
[793](#793)    AtomicU64_le AtomicU64_be: 8 AtomicU64 as u64,
[794](#794)}

[802](#802)    #[test]
[803](#803)    fn signed_integers() {
[804](#804)        assert_size_align! {
[805](#805)            i16_be 2 2,
[806](#806)            i16_le 2 2,
[807](#807)            i32_be 4 4,
[808](#808)            i32_le 4 4,
[809](#809)            i64_be 8 8,
[810](#810)            i64_le 8 8,
[811](#811)            i128_be 16 16,
[812](#812)            i128_le 16 16,
[813](#813)        }
[814](#814)
[815](#815)        unsafe {
[816](#816)            assert_eq!(
[818](#818)                [0x02, 0x01],
[819](#819)                transmute::<_, [u8; 2]>(i16_le::from_native(0x0102)),
[820](#820)            );
[821](#821)            assert_eq!(
[822](#822)                [0x01, 0x02],
[823](#823)                transmute::<_, [u8; 2]>(i16_be::from_native(0x0102)),
[824](#824)            );
[825](#825)
[826](#826)            assert_eq!(
[828](#828)                [0x04, 0x03, 0x02, 0x01],
[829](#829)                transmute::<_, [u8; 4]>(i32_le::from_native(0x01020304)),
[830](#830)            );
[831](#831)            assert_eq!(
[832](#832)                [0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x04],
[833](#833)                transmute::<_, [u8; 4]>(i32_be::from_native(0x01020304)),
[834](#834)            );
[835](#835)
[836](#836)            assert_eq!(
[838](#838)                [0x08, 0x07, 0x06, 0x05, 0x04, 0x03, 0x02, 0x01],
[839](#839)                transmute::<_, [u8; 8]>(i64_le::from_native(
[840](#840)                    0x0102030405060708
[841](#841)                )),
[842](#842)            );
[843](#843)            assert_eq!(
[844](#844)                [0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x04, 0x05, 0x06, 0x07, 0x08],
[845](#845)                transmute::<_, [u8; 8]>(i64_be::from_native(
[846](#846)                    0x0102030405060708
[847](#847)                )),
[848](#848)            );
[849](#849)
[850](#850)            assert_eq!(
[852](#852)                [
[853](#853)                    0x10, 0x0f, 0x0e, 0x0d, 0x0c, 0x0b, 0x0a, 0x09, 0x08, 0x07,
[854](#854)                    0x06, 0x05, 0x04, 0x03, 0x02, 0x01
[855](#855)                ],
[856](#856)                transmute::<_, [u8; 16]>(i128_le::from_native(
[857](#857)                    0x0102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f10
[858](#858)                )),
[859](#859)            );
[860](#860)            assert_eq!(
[861](#861)                [
[862](#862)                    0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x04, 0x05, 0x06, 0x07, 0x08, 0x09, 0x0a,
[863](#863)                    0x0b, 0x0c, 0x0d, 0x0e, 0x0f, 0x10
[864](#864)                ],
[865](#865)                transmute::<_, [u8; 16]>(i128_be::from_native(
[866](#866)                    0x0102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f10
[867](#867)                )),
[868](#868)            );
[869](#869)        }
[870](#870)    }

[944](#944)        assert_size_align! {

[946](#946)            f32_le 4 4,
[947](#947)            f64_be 8 8,
[948](#948)            f64_le 8 8,
[949](#949)        }
[950](#950)
[951](#951)        unsafe {
[952](#952)            assert_eq!(
[954](#954)                [0xdb, 0x0f, 0x49, 0x40],
[955](#955)                transmute::<_, [u8; 4]>(f32_le::from_native(
[956](#956)                    core::f32::consts::PI
[957](#957)                )),
[958](#958)            );
[959](#959)            assert_eq!(
[960](#960)                [0x40, 0x49, 0x0f, 0xdb],
[961](#961)                transmute::<_, [u8; 4]>(f32_be::from_native(
[962](#962)                    core::f32::consts::PI
[963](#963)                )),
[964](#964)            );
[965](#965)
[966](#966)            assert_eq!(
[968](#968)                [0x18, 0x2d, 0x44, 0x54, 0xfb, 0x21, 0x09, 0x40],

[970](#970)                    core::f64::consts::PI
[971](#971)                )),
[972](#972)            );
[973](#973)            assert_eq!(
[974](#974)                [0x40, 0x09, 0x21, 0xfb, 0x54, 0x44, 0x2d, 0x18],
[975](#975)                transmute::<_, [u8; 8]>(f64_be::from_native(
[976](#976)                    core::f64::consts::PI
[977](#977)                )),
[978](#978)            );
[979](#979)
[980](#980)            assert_eq!(
[982](#982)                [0x89, 0xf3, 0x01, 0x00],
[983](#983)                transmute::<_, [u8; 4]>(char_le::from_native('🎉')),
[984](#984)            );
[985](#985)            assert_eq!(
[986](#986)                [0x00, 0x01, 0xf3, 0x89],
[987](#987)                transmute::<_, [u8; 4]>(char_be::from_native('🎉')),
[988](#988)            );
[989](#989)        }

[993](#993)    fn signed_non_zero() {
[994](#994)        assert_size_align! {
[995](#995)            NonZeroI16_le 2 2,

[997](#997)            NonZeroI32_le 4 4,
[998](#998)            NonZeroI32_be 4 4,
[999](#999)            NonZeroI64_le 8 8,
[1000](#1000)            NonZeroI64_be 8 8,
[1001](#1001)            NonZeroI128_le 16 16,
[1002](#1002)            NonZeroI128_be 16 16,
[1003](#1003)        }
[1004](#1004)
[1005](#1005)        unsafe {
[1006](#1006)            assert_eq!(
[1008](#1008)                [0x02, 0x01],
[1009](#1009)                transmute::<_, [u8; 2]>(NonZeroI16_le::new_unchecked(0x0102)),
[1010](#1010)            );
[1011](#1011)            assert_eq!(
[1012](#1012)                [0x01, 0x02],

[1014](#1014)            );

[1016](#1016)            assert_eq!(
[1018](#1018)                [0x04, 0x03, 0x02, 0x01],

[1020](#1020)                    0x01020304
[1021](#1021)                )),
[1022](#1022)            );
[1023](#1023)            assert_eq!(
[1024](#1024)                [0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x04],
[1025](#1025)                transmute::<_, [u8; 4]>(NonZeroI32_be::new_unchecked(
[1026](#1026)                    0x01020304
[1027](#1027)                )),
[1028](#1028)            );
[1029](#1029)
[1030](#1030)            assert_eq!(
[1032](#1032)                [0x08, 0x07, 0x06, 0x05, 0x04, 0x03, 0x02, 0x01],

[1034](#1034)                    0x0102030405060708
[1035](#1035)                )),
[1036](#1036)            );
[1037](#1037)            assert_eq!(
[1038](#1038)                [0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x04, 0x05, 0x06, 0x07, 0x08],
[1039](#1039)                transmute::<_, [u8; 8]>(NonZeroI64_be::new_unchecked(
[1040](#1040)                    0x0102030405060708
[1041](#1041)                )),
[1042](#1042)            );
[1043](#1043)
[1044](#1044)            assert_eq!(
[1046](#1046)                [
[1047](#1047)                    0x10, 0x0f, 0x0e, 0x0d, 0x0c, 0x0b, 0x0a, 0x09, 0x08, 0x07,
[1048](#1048)                    0x06, 0x05, 0x04, 0x03, 0x02, 0x01
[1049](#1049)                ],
[1050](#1050)                transmute::<_, [u8; 16]>(NonZeroI128_le::new_unchecked(
[1051](#1051)                    0x0102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f10
[1052](#1052)                )),
[1053](#1053)            );
[1054](#1054)            assert_eq!(
[1055](#1055)                [
[1056](#1056)                    0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x04, 0x05, 0x06, 0x07, 0x08, 0x09, 0x0a,
[1057](#1057)                    0x0b, 0x0c, 0x0d, 0x0e, 0x0f, 0x10
[1058](#1058)                ],
[1059](#1059)                transmute::<_, [u8; 16]>(NonZeroI128_be::new_unchecked(

[1061](#1061)                )),

# rend::unaligned - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rend/0.5.4/rend/unaligned/index.html

## Expand description

Cross-platform primitives with unaligned representations.

# AtomicI16_be in rend - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rend/0.5.4/rend/struct.AtomicI16_be.html

`pub struct AtomicI16_be(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

A big-endian `AtomicI16` with a guaranteed size and alignment of `2`.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rend/lib.rs.html#779-782)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-AtomicI16_be-1)### impl [AtomicI16_be](https://docs.rs/struct.AtomicI16_be.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rend/lib.rs.html#779-782)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-AtomicI16_be-1)

### impl [AtomicI16_be](https://docs.rs/struct.AtomicI16_be.html)

Adds to the current value, returning the previous value.

Because addition is not an endian-agnostic operation, `fetch_add` is implemented in terms of [ AtomicI16::compare_exchange_weak](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/struct.Atomic.html#method.compare_exchange_weak) on little-endian targets. This may result in worse performance on those targets.

See [ AtomicI16::fetch_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/struct.Atomic.html#method.fetch_add) for more information.

Maximum with the current value.

Because maximum is not an endian-agnostic operation, `fetch_max` is implemented in terms of [ AtomicI16::compare_exchange_weak](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/struct.Atomic.html#method.compare_exchange_weak) on little-endian targets. This may result in worse performance on those targets.

See [ AtomicI16::fetch_max](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/struct.Atomic.html#method.fetch_max) for more information.

Minimum with the current value.

Because minimum is not an endian-agnostic operation, `fetch_min` is implemented in terms of [ AtomicI16::compare_exchange_weak](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/struct.Atomic.html#method.compare_exchange_weak) on little-endian targets. This may result in worse performance on those targets.

See [ AtomicI16::fetch_min](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/struct.Atomic.html#method.fetch_min) for more information.

Subtracts from the current value, returning the previous value.

Because subtraction is not an endian-agnostic operation, `fetch_sub` is implemented in terms of [ AtomicI16::compare_exchange_weak](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/struct.Atomic.html#method.compare_exchange_weak) on little-endian targets. This may result in worse performance on those targets.

See [ AtomicI16::fetch_sub](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/struct.Atomic.html#method.fetch_sub) for more information.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rend/lib.rs.html#779-782)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rend/lib.rs.html#779-782)

Fetches the value, and applies a function to it that returns an
optional new value. Returns a `Result` of `Ok(previous_value)`
if the function returned `Some(_)`, else `Err(previous_value)`.

See [ AtomicI16::fetch_update](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/struct.Atomic.html#method.fetch_update) for more information.

### impl [AtomicI32_be](https://docs.rs/struct.AtomicI32_be.html)

Adds to the current value, returning the previous value.

Because addition is not an endian-agnostic operation, `fetch_add` is implemented in terms of [ AtomicI32::compare_exchange_weak](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/struct.Atomic.html#method.compare_exchange_weak) on little-endian targets. This may result in worse performance on those targets.

See [ AtomicI32::fetch_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/struct.Atomic.html#method.fetch_add) for more information.

Maximum with the current value.

Because maximum is not an endian-agnostic operation, `fetch_max` is implemented in terms of [ AtomicI32::compare_exchange_weak](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/struct.Atomic.html#method.compare_exchange_weak) on little-endian targets. This may result in worse performance on those targets.

See [ AtomicI32::fetch_max](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/struct.Atomic.html#method.fetch_max) for more information.

Minimum with the current value.

Because minimum is not an endian-agnostic operation, `fetch_min` is implemented in terms of [ AtomicI32::compare_exchange_weak](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/struct.Atomic.html#method.compare_exchange_weak) on little-endian targets. This may result in worse performance on those targets.

See [ AtomicI32::fetch_min](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/struct.Atomic.html#method.fetch_min) for more information.

Subtracts from the current value, returning the previous value.

Because subtraction is not an endian-agnostic operation, `fetch_sub` is implemented in terms of [ AtomicI32::compare_exchange_weak](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/struct.Atomic.html#method.compare_exchange_weak) on little-endian targets. This may result in worse performance on those targets.

See [ AtomicI32::fetch_sub](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/struct.Atomic.html#method.fetch_sub) for more information.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rend/lib.rs.html#785-788)

Fetches the value, and applies a function to it that returns an
optional new value. Returns a `Result` of `Ok(previous_value)`
if the function returned `Some(_)`, else `Err(previous_value)`.

See [ AtomicI32::fetch_update](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/struct.Atomic.html#method.fetch_update) for more information.

# Struct NonZeroI16_be

[Source](../src/rend/lib.rs.html#318-327) `pub struct NonZeroI16_be();`

## Expand description

A big-endian `NonZeroI16` with a guaranteed size and alignment of `2`.

Creates a non-zero if the given value is not zero.

Creates a non-zero without checking whether it is non-zero. This
results in undefined behavior if the value is zero.

# rend - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rend/latest/rend/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rend)rend

rend provides cross-platform, endian-aware primitives for Rust.

rend does not provide cross-platform alternatives for types that are
inherently cross-platform, such as `bool` and `u8`. It also does not provide
cross-platform alternatives for types that have an architecture-dependent
size, such as `isize` and `usize`. rend does not support custom types.

rend is intended to be used to build portable types that can be shared between different architectures.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `bytecheck`: Enables support for validating types using- `bytecheck`.

[§](https://docs.rs#crates)Crates

- `zerocopy-0_8`

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example:

```
use core::mem::transmute;
use rend::*;
let little_int = i32_le::from_native(0x12345678);
// Internal representation is little-endian
assert_eq!(
    [0x78, 0x56, 0x34, 0x12],
    unsafe { transmute::<_, [u8; 4]>(little_int) }
);
// Can also be made with `.into()`
let little_int: i32_le = 0x12345678.into();
// Still formats correctly
assert_eq!("305419896", format!("{}", little_int));
assert_eq!("0x12345678", format!("0x{:x}", little_int));
let big_int = i32_be::from_native(0x12345678);
// Internal representation is big-endian
assert_eq!(
    [0x12, 0x34, 0x56, 0x78],
    unsafe { transmute::<_, [u8; 4]>(big_int) }
);
// Can also be made with `.into()`
let big_int: i32_be = 0x12345678.into();
// Still formats correctly
assert_eq!("305419896", format!("{}", big_int));
assert_eq!("0x12345678", format!("0x{:x}", big_int));
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [unaligned](https://docs.rs/unaligned/index.html)
- Cross-platform primitives with unaligned representations.

# rend 0.5.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rend/latest/builds

All the builds on docs.rs are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The limits for this crate are the following:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                    If a build fails because it hit one of those limits please
                    [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                    to get them increased.

# bytemuck 1.25.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bytemuck/^1

# bytemuck

A crate for mucking around with piles of bytes.

This crate lets you safely perform "bit cast" operations between data types. That's where you take a value and just reinterpret the bits as being some other type of value, without changing the bits.

- This is **not**like the`as`keyword
- This is **not**like the`From`trait
- It is **most like**`f32::to_bits`

### Here's the part you're more likely to care about: *you can do this with slices too!*

When a slice is involved it's not a *direct* bitcast. Instead, the `cast_slice`
and `cast_slice_mut` functions will pull apart a slice's data and give you a new
slice that's the same span of memory just viewed as the new type. If the size of
the slice's element changes then the length of the slice you get back will be
changed accordingly.

This lets you cast a slice of color values into a slice of `u8` and send it to
the GPU, or things like that. I'm sure there's other examples, but honestly this
crate is as popular as it is mostly because of Rust's 3D graphics community
wanting to cast slices of different types into byte slices for sending to the
GPU. Hi friends! Push those vertices, or whatever it is that you all do.

## See Also

While `bytemuck` is full of unsafe code, I've also started a "sibling crate"
called [bitfrob](https://docs.rs/bitfrob/latest/bitfrob/), which is where
operations that are 100% safe will be added.

## Stability

- The crate is 1.0 and I consider this it to be "basically done". New features
are usually being accepted when other people want to put in the work, but
myself I wanna move on to using `bytemuck`in bigger projects.
- The default build of the `bytemuck`crate will continue to work with`rustc-1.34`for at least the rest of the`1.y.z`versions.
- Any other cargo features of the crate **are not**held to the same standard, and may work only on the latest Stable or even only on latest Nightly.

**Future Plans:** Once the [Safe Transmute Project](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2835-project-safe-transmute.html) completes and
stabilizes ("eventually") this crate will be updated to use that as the
underlying mechanism for transmutation bounds, and a 2.0 version of `bytemuck`
will be released. The hope is for the 1.0 to 2.0 transition to be as seamless as
possible, but the future is always uncertain.

---

# zerocopy 0.8.52 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/zerocopy/^0.8

# zerocopy

**Fast, safe, compile error. Pick two.**

Zerocopy makes zero-cost memory manipulation effortless. We write `unsafe`
so you don't have to.

*For an overview of what's changed from zerocopy 0.7, check out our  release
notes, which include a step-by-step upgrading guide.*

*Have questions? Need more out of zerocopy? Submit a  customer request
issue or ask the maintainers on
GitHub or Discord!*

## Overview

###### Conversion Traits

Zerocopy provides four derivable traits for zero-cost conversions:

- `TryFromBytes`indicates that a type may safely be converted from certain byte sequences (conditional on runtime checks)
- `FromZeros`indicates that a sequence of zero bytes represents a valid instance of a type
- `FromBytes`indicates that a type may safely be converted from an arbitrary byte sequence
- `IntoBytes`indicates that a type may safely be converted- *to*a byte sequence

These traits support sized types, slices, and [slice DSTs](https://docs.rs/KnownLayout#dynamically-sized-types).

###### Marker Traits

Zerocopy provides three derivable marker traits that do not provide any functionality themselves, but are required to call certain methods provided by the conversion traits:

- `KnownLayout`indicates that zerocopy can reason about certain layout qualities of a type
- `Immutable`indicates that a type is free from interior mutability, except by ownership or an exclusive (- `&mut`) borrow
- `Unaligned`indicates that a type's alignment requirement is 1

You should generally derive these marker traits whenever possible.

###### Conversion Macros

Zerocopy provides six macros for safe casting between types:

- (`try_`[try_transmute])`transmute`(conditionally) converts a value of one type to a value of another type of the same size
- (`try_`[try_transmute_mut])`transmute_mut`(conditionally) converts a mutable reference of one type to a mutable reference of another type of the same size
- (`try_`[try_transmute_ref])`transmute_ref`(conditionally) converts a mutable or immutable reference of one type to an immutable reference of another type of the same size

These macros perform *compile-time* size and alignment checks, meaning that
unconditional casts have zero cost at runtime. Conditional casts do not need
to validate size or alignment runtime, but do need to validate contents.

These macros cannot be used in generic contexts. For generic conversions,
use the methods defined by the [conversion traits](https://docs.rs#conversion-traits).

###### Byteorder-Aware Numerics

Zerocopy provides byte-order aware integer types that support these
conversions; see the `byteorder` module. These types are especially useful
for network parsing.

## Cargo Features

-
`alloc``zerocopy`is`no_std`. When the`alloc`feature is enabled, the`alloc`crate is added as a dependency, and some allocation-related functionality is added.
-
`std``zerocopy`is`no_std`. When the`std`feature is enabled, the`std`crate is added as a dependency (ie,`no_std`is disabled), and support for some`std`types is added.`std`implies`alloc`.
-
`derive``zerocopy-derive`crate. These derives are re-exported from`zerocopy`, so it is not necessary to depend on`zerocopy-derive`directly.However, you may experience better compile times if you instead directly depend on both `zerocopy`and`zerocopy-derive`in your`Cargo.toml`, since doing so will allow Rust to compile these crates in parallel. To do so, do*not*enable the`derive`feature, and list both dependencies in your`Cargo.toml`with the same leading non-zero version number; e.g:`[] = "0.X" = "0.X"`To avoid the risk of [duplicate import errors](https://github.com/google/zerocopy/issues/1587)if one of your dependencies enables zerocopy's`derive`feature, import derives as`use zerocopy_derive::*`rather than by name (e.g.,`use zerocopy_derive::FromBytes`).
-
`simd``simd`feature is enabled,`FromZeros`,`FromBytes`, and`IntoBytes`impls are emitted for all stable SIMD types which exist on the target platform. Note that the layout of SIMD types is not yet stabilized, so these impls may be removed in the future if layout changes make them invalid. For more information, see the Unsafe Code Guidelines Reference page on the[layout of packed SIMD vectors](https://rust-lang.github.io/unsafe-code-guidelines/layout/packed-simd-vectors.html).
-
`simd-nightly``simd`feature and adds support for SIMD types which are only available on nightly. Since these types are unstable, support for any type may be removed at any point in the future.
-
`float-nightly``f16`and`f128`types. These types are not yet fully implemented and may not be supported on all platforms.

## Build Tuning

`--cfg zerocopy_inline_always`

Upgrades `#[inline]` to `#[inline(always)]` on many of zerocopy's public
functions and methods. This provides a narrowly-scoped alternative that
*may* improve the optimization of hot paths using zerocopy without the broad
compile-time penalties of configuring `codegen-units=1`.

## Security Ethos

Zerocopy is expressly designed for use in security-critical contexts. We
strive to ensure that that zerocopy code is sound under Rust's current
memory model, and *any future memory model*. We ensure this by:

- **...not 'guessing' about Rust's semantics.**We annotate- `unsafe`code with a precise rationale for its soundness that cites a relevant section of Rust's official documentation. When Rust's documented semantics are unclear, we work with the Rust Operational Semantics Team to clarify Rust's documentation.
- **...rigorously testing our implementation.**We run tests using- [Miri](https://github.com/rust-lang/miri), ensuring that zerocopy is sound across a wide array of supported target platforms of varying endianness and pointer width, and across both current and experimental memory models of Rust.
- **...formally proving the correctness of our implementation.**We apply formal verification tools like- [Kani](https://github.com/model-checking/kani)to prove zerocopy's correctness.

For more information, see our full [soundness policy](https://github.com/google/zerocopy/blob/main/zerocopy/POLICIES.md#soundness).

## Relationship to Project Safe Transmute

[Project Safe Transmute](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2835-project-safe-transmute.html) is an official initiative of the Rust Project to
develop language-level support for safer transmutation. The Project consults
with crates like zerocopy to identify aspects of safer transmutation that
would benefit from compiler support, and has developed an [experimental,
compiler-supported analysis](https://github.com/rust-lang/compiler-team/issues/411) which determines whether,
for a given type, any value of that type may be soundly transmuted into
another type. Once this functionality is sufficiently mature, zerocopy
intends to replace its internal transmutability analysis (implemented by our
custom derives) with the compiler-supported one. This change will likely be
an implementation detail that is invisible to zerocopy's users.

Project Safe Transmute will not replace the need for most of zerocopy's
higher-level abstractions. The experimental compiler analysis is a tool for
checking the soundness of `unsafe` code, not a tool to avoid writing
`unsafe` code altogether. For the foreseeable future, crates like zerocopy
will still be required in order to provide higher-level abstractions on top
of the building block provided by Project Safe Transmute.

## MSRV

See our [MSRV policy](https://github.com/google/zerocopy/blob/main/zerocopy/POLICIES.md#msrv).

## Changelog

Zerocopy uses [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/google/zerocopy/releases).

## Thanks

Zerocopy is maintained by engineers at Google with help from [many wonderful
contributors](https://github.com/google/zerocopy/graphs/contributors). Thank you to everyone who has lent a hand in
making Rust a little more secure!

## Disclaimer

Disclaimer: Zerocopy is not an officially supported Google product.

---

# rend 0.5.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rend/0.5.3

`rend`

rend provides cross-platform, endian-aware primitives for Rust.

## Documentation

- [rend](https://docs.rs/rend), provides cross-platform, endian-aware primitives for Rust

## Example

```
use transmute;
use *;
let little_int = from_native;
// Internal representation is little-endian
assert_eq!;
// Can also be made with `.into()`
let little_int: i32_le = 0x12345678.into;
// Still formats correctly
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
let big_int = from_native;
// Internal representation is big-endian
assert_eq!;
// Can also be made with `.into()`
let big_int: i32_be = 0x12345678.into;
// Still formats correctly
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```

---

let little_int: i32_le = 0x12345678.into;
// Still formats correctly
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
let big_int = new;
// Internal representation is big-endian
assert_eq!;
// Can also be made with `.into()`
let big_int: i32_be = 0x12345678.into;
// Still formats correctly
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```

# rend - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rend

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rend)rend

rend provides cross-platform, endian-aware primitives for Rust.

rend does not provide cross-platform alternatives for types that are
inherently cross-platform, such as `bool` and `u8`. It also does not provide
cross-platform alternatives for types that have an architecture-dependent
size, such as `isize` and `usize`. rend does not support custom types.

rend is intended to be used to build portable types that can be shared between different architectures.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `bytecheck`: Enables support for validating types using- `bytecheck`.

[§](https://docs.rs#crates)Crates

- `zerocopy-0_8`

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example:

```
use core::mem::transmute;
use rend::*;
let little_int = i32_le::from_native(0x12345678);
// Internal representation is little-endian
assert_eq!(
    [0x78, 0x56, 0x34, 0x12],
    unsafe { transmute::<_, [u8; 4]>(little_int) }
);
// Can also be made with `.into()`
let little_int: i32_le = 0x12345678.into();
// Still formats correctly
assert_eq!("305419896", format!("{}", little_int));
assert_eq!("0x12345678", format!("0x{:x}", little_int));
let big_int = i32_be::from_native(0x12345678);
// Internal representation is big-endian
assert_eq!(
    [0x12, 0x34, 0x56, 0x78],
    unsafe { transmute::<_, [u8; 4]>(big_int) }
);
// Can also be made with `.into()`
let big_int: i32_be = 0x12345678.into();
// Still formats correctly
assert_eq!("305419896", format!("{}", big_int));
assert_eq!("0x12345678", format!("0x{:x}", big_int));
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [unaligned](https://docs.rs/unaligned/index.html)
- Cross-platform primitives with unaligned representations.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Atomic](https://docs.rs/struct.AtomicI16_be.html)- I16_ - be
- A big-endian `AtomicI16`with a guaranteed size and alignment of`2`.
- [Atomic](https://docs.rs/struct.AtomicI16_le.html)- I16_ - le
- A little-endian `AtomicI16`with a guaranteed size and alignment of`2`.
- [Atomic](https://docs.rs/struct.AtomicI32_be.html)- I32_ - be

- [Atomic](https://docs.rs/struct.AtomicI32_le.html)- I32_ - le

# rend 0.5.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rend/latest/source/rustfmt.toml

#
                    rend 0.5.4

                Cross-platform, endian-aware primitives for Rust

# ptr_meta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ptr_meta/^0.3/

## Expand description

A radioactive stabilization of the [ ptr_meta RFC](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2580-ptr-meta.html).

This crate provides the [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) trait,

[and](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html)

`from_raw_parts`[functions, and proc macros for deriving](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html)

`to_raw_parts``Pointee` for
structs and implementing `Pointee` for trait objects.[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Raw pointers can be decomposed into the data address and metadata components
with [ to_raw_parts](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html) or

[.](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts_mut.html)

`to_raw_parts_mut`Alternatively, metadata alone can be extracted with the [ metadata](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)
function. Although

[accepts pointers, references can be passed and will be implicitly coerced.](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)

`metadata`A pointer can be created from its address and metadata with
[ from_raw_parts](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html) or

[.](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts_mut.html)

`from_raw_parts_mut`[§](https://docs.rs#provided-impls)Provided impls

`ptr_meta` provides inherent implementations for many builtin types:

- All `Sized``Pointee`
- `slice`,- `str`, and- `CStr`
- `OsStr`(requires- `std`)
- `dyn Any`, optionally with- `+ Send`and/or- `+ Sync`
- `dyn Error`, optionally with- `+ Send`and/or- `+ Sync`

[§](https://docs.rs#structs-with-trailing-dsts)Structs with trailing DSTs

You can derive [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) for structs with trailing DSTs:

```
use ptr_meta::Pointee;
#[derive(Pointee)]
struct Block<H, T> {
    header: H,
    elements: [T],
}
```
Note that the last field is required to be a DST. Structs with a generic
type as the last field may have conflicting blanket implementations, as the
generic type may be `Sized`. A collection of specific implementations may be
required in these cases, with the generic parameter set (for example) a
slice, `str`, or specific trait object.

[§](https://docs.rs#trait-objects)Trait objects

You can generate [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) implementations for trait objects:

```
use ptr_meta::pointee;
// Generates Pointee for dyn Stringy
#[ptr_meta::pointee]
trait Stringy {
    fn as_string(&self) -> String;
}
```
Note that this will not produce implementations for `Trait + Send + Sync`.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `derive`: Re-exports the macros from- `ptr_meta_derive`. Enabled by default.
- `std`: Enables additional impls for- `std`types. Enabled by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
// Get the associated metadata for pointers
let str = "hello world";
assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata(str), str.len());
let slice = &[1, 2, 3, 4, 5] as &[i32];
assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata(slice), slice.len());
// Make your own wide pointers from data pointers and metadata
let bytes = [b'h', b'e', b'l', b'l', b'o'];
let ptr = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<str>(bytes.as_ptr().cast(), 5);
println!("{} world!", unsafe { &*ptr }); // prints "hello world!"
// Derive Pointee on your own types
#[derive(ptr_meta::Pointee)]
#[repr(transparent)]
struct CoolStr {
    inner: str,
}
impl CoolStr {
    fn print_cool(&self) {
        println!("😎 {} 😎", &self.inner);
    }
}
let ptr = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<CoolStr>(bytes.as_ptr().cast(), 5);
let cool = unsafe { &*ptr };
cool.print_cool(); // prints "😎 hello 😎"
// Implement Pointee for trait objects
#[ptr_meta::pointee]
trait Printable {
    fn print(&self);
}
impl Printable for i32 {
    fn print(&self) {
        println!("i32: {self}");
    }
}
let i32_vtable = ptr_meta::metadata(&0i32 as &dyn Printable);
let one_hundred = 100i32;
let printable = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<dyn Printable>(
    (&one_hundred as *const i32).cast(),
    i32_vtable,
);
unsafe {
    (*printable).print(); // prints "i32: 100"
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [DynMetadata](https://docs.rs/struct.DynMetadata.html)
- The metadata for a trait object.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html)
- A trait which associates pointer metadata with a pointee type.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html)- raw_ - parts
- Returns a raw pointer with the given data address and metadata.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts_mut.html)- raw_ - parts_ - mut
- Returns a mutable raw pointer with the given data address and metadata.
- [metadata](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)
- Returns the metadata of the given pointer.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html)- raw_ - parts
- Returns the data address and metadata of the given pointer.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts_mut.html)- raw_ - parts_ - mut
- Returns the mutable data address and metadata of the given pointer.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [pointee](https://docs.rs/attr.pointee.html)- `derive`
- Generates a `Pointee`implementation for trait object of the labeled trait.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Pointee](https://docs.rs/derive.Pointee.html)- `derive`
- Derives `Pointee`for the labeled struct which has a trailing DST.

# rancor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rancor/^0.1/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rancor)rancor

rancor provides scalable and efficient error handling without using type composition. This makes it best-suited for situations where:

- Programmatic error introspection is not useful
- Functions may error, but succeed most of the time
- Errors should provide as much useful detail as possible when emitted
- Use cases include both `no_std`and targets with support for`std`

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `alloc`: Provides the- `BoxedError`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [fail](https://docs.rs/macro.fail.html)
- Returns the given error from this function.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Boxed](https://docs.rs/struct.BoxedError.html)- Error - `alloc`
- An error type that preserves all detailed error messages. It is optimized to fit in a single pointer.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- A good general-purpose error type.
- [Failure](https://docs.rs/struct.Failure.html)
- An error type that only preserves success or failure, throwing away any more detailed error messages.
- [Strategy](https://docs.rs/struct.Strategy.html)
- Equips a type with a `Fallible`implementation that chooses`E`as its error type.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Infallible](https://docs.rs/enum.Infallible.html)
- A re-export of `core::convert::Infallible`. The error type for errors that can never happen.
- [Panic](https://docs.rs/enum.Panic.html)
- An error type that does not occupy any space, panicking on creation instead.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Fallible](https://docs.rs/trait.Fallible.html)
- A type with fallible operations that return its associated error type.
- [Never](https://docs.rs/trait.Never.html)
- A type that can never be produced.
- [Option](https://docs.rs/trait.OptionExt.html)- Ext
- Helper methods for `Option`s.
- [Result](https://docs.rs/trait.ResultExt.html)- Ext
- Helper methods for `Result`s.
- [Source](https://docs.rs/trait.Source.html)
- An error type which can be uniformly constructed from an `Error`
- [Trace](https://docs.rs/trait.Trace.html)
- An error type which can add additional “trace” information to itself.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [unreachable_](https://docs.rs/fn.unreachable_checked.html)- checked
- Consumes a `Never`type, returning a primitive`!`.
